title: A day accounted for
hook: Seneca gives his day: a cold plunge, a short run, dry bread, a nap (Letters 83)

segments.voice: Yesterday: persona. Your line was behind the mask. Whose costume did you look past, and what did you find? Day four hundred seventy-four.

What do you actually do all day? What time do you get up? What do you eat? It's what we ask anyone whose life we're curious about, and it's what Lucilius has asked Seneca. In the eighty-third letter, Seneca answers, hour by hour, with surprising honesty and quite a lot of humor at his own expense. What comes back is a day in the life of an aging Roman philosopher, and it's very ordinary. Today: a day accounted for.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?` → `HOUR BY HOUR, HONESTLY.` → `A DAY IN AN OLD PHILOSOPHER'S LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, why tell it. We should live, Seneca says, as if we lived in plain sight, as if God could look into our hearts at any time. So he'll watch himself and review his day, which he calls a most useful practice. Today, he says, is whole: nobody stole any of it. Second, the run. He's taken up a little running, with a young slave named Pharius as his partner. They're at the same turning point, he jokes, since both of them are losing teeth, and soon he won't be able to keep up. Third, the plunge. Seneca was once a great cold-water bather. He used to greet the first of January with a plunge into the canal. Then he moved to the Tiber. Then to a tub. And now, he confesses, it's a tub the sun has warmed, on his bravest days. That's an old man's honest report. Fourth, the meal and the nap. Lunch is dry bread, with no table needed, and so simple there's no washing of hands afterward. Then a very short nap. Nothing heroic. What's striking is the honesty. He doesn't polish the day. He shows the decline, the jokes, the plain bread. Accounting for a day like that isn't about judging it. It's about seeing where it actually went.
screen: `LIVE AS IF IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `A RACE WITH PHARIUS.` · `CANAL, RIVER, TUB, WARM WATER.` · `DRY BREAD AND A SHORT NAP.` · then, large: `MY DAY, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Walk back through today so far, the way Seneca does, hour by hour. When did you wake? What came first: the phone, a coffee, a person? What did you eat? Where did the middle of the day go? Don't polish it and don't scold it. Just let the timetable appear, as it really was. Notice one hour that was wholly yours, and one that got stolen. The bell holds the time.
Dies solidus. Latin for an unbroken day: Seneca reports his own, hour by hour, a run, a plunge, dry bread, a nap, to see where it went. Today's word.
Your line: my day, honestly. Tonight, write today's timetable in a few plain lines, with no polishing. Mark the hour that was wholly yours. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners write a plain account of their day in the evening, noting where the hours went without praising or scolding themselves.

fork.setup: Lucilius asks what you do all day. you're an aging philosopher who's slowed down a lot. what do you write?
options: a heroic schedule to inspire him.
the honest timetable, including the warm bath and the nap.
fork.reveal: Seneca reports it all, with jokes about his teeth and his softening plunge: an honest account, not a polished one.

original.note: Latin: an unbroken day. Seneca says in Letters 83.3 that today is unbroken, with nothing stolen from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics live heroic, ice-cold, iron routines.
what it means: Seneca's day is plain and honestly told; the point is to see where it went.
what a scholar hears: Letters 83.1–6; the daily self-review echoes On Anger 3.36, where Seneca describes examining each day at night, following the philosopher Sextius.

notes: Letters 83.1–2: live as if in plain sight, God sees within; 83.2–3 'dies integer est', self-observation and review of the day. 83.4: running with Pharius, both losing teeth. 83.5: from the Euripus (canal) on the Kalends of January, to the Tiber, to a tub, to warm water. 83.6: dry bread, no table, no washing of hands, a very short sleep. Editor review (2026-10-01): the original-language phrase was wrong: 83.3 reads 'hodiernus dies solidus est', not 'integer'; corrected. Sextius was not Seneca's own teacher (Seneca studied under Sotion, a Sextian); trapdoor fixed. Cut the unsourced superlative 'the closest thing we have to a day in the life'. The Pharius joke now follows 83.4 (same crisis, both losing teeth, soon he can't keep up) rather than 'he'll need a younger runner'. 83.5's plunge: New Year's Day canal, then the Tiber, then a sun-warmed tub 'cum fortissimus sum'; 'as a younger man' removed. Hook reopened with the question to vary from day 472's 'Lucilius is sick' opener. Confirm 83.4 wording.
